solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Theresa May dancing; senior Tory unfortunately starts to join in – it's "somewhat beneath Essex"

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only the first of each word is kept
dancers move about, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: the name taken as written
the first letter of each of these three words

explanation.surface: The former Prime Minister does one of her famously awkward dances while a senior Conservative grimly joins in.
explanation.walkthrough: Theresa May was a Conservative Prime Minister known for stiff dancing. Essex is a county east of London; the estuary where the Thames widens into the sea lies along its southern edge.
explanation.definitionFit: The tidal mouth of London's river forms the southern border of that county, so it lies somewhat below it on a map.

clue.text: Agitated male set about

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: the male pronoun
to set something down is to put it

explanation.surface: A worked-up man is getting ready to lay into someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set about' reads as one phrasal verb meaning attack, but it splits into a verb and a turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worked up is an informal British phrase for feeling anxious, excited or upset.

clue.text: Notes from mad remoaner about to go bananas

indicators.note: letters that go are removed, so they are dropped from the word
going bananas is going crazy, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written before the cut
RE is Latin for 'about', concerning

explanation.surface: A furious Remain supporter scribbles notes about to lose their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: A remoaner is a scornful British name for someone still complaining about the Brexit vote. 'About to go' looks like 'nearly going'; here 'about' is RE and 'to go' removes it from the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda is the Latin plural of memorandum, written reminders or short business messages.

clue.text: Corbyn finally intervenes in rift, which keeps injured member in line

definitions.text: which keeps injured member in line

indicators.note: what comes finally is the last thing, so only the closing letter is kept
to intervene is to come between, so one piece is set inside another

blocks.note: a rift in a party is a split
the last letter of the name

explanation.surface: The Labour leader at last steps into a party split to keep a wounded member toeing the line.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn led the Labour Party. 'Member' and 'in line' read as party discipline, but the member is a limb and the line is keeping a broken bone straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigid strip strapped to a broken limb holds the bone straight while it heals.

clue.text: My! Boris, changing political sides, is playing with Conservative representative

indicators.note: switching from right to left swaps one side's letter for the other's
playing about with letters rearranges them freely

blocks.note: taken as written
the name with its R (right) replaced by L (left)
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Astonishment that Boris Johnson has defected and is toying with a Tory MP.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L stand for right and left, so swapping political sides turns R into L. Boris Johnson was a Conservative Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Something symbolic stands for something else, as a representative stands in for others.

clue.text: see 17dn.
Bill's necking or getting screwed

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted out of shape, so the letters are wrenched round

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Bill is either kissing or having sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is the account presented for payment.
explanation.definitionFit: A reckoning is an old word for an account or invoice, especially one totted up at an inn.

clue.text: Pressure former princess to get out of trouble

indicators.note: what gets out leaves, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: to trouble someone is to distress them
Princess Diana, popularly called Di

explanation.surface: Someone leans on a one-time royal to escape her difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressure' looks like a verb at the start of an instruction, but it is the noun being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress and pressure are both physical force and the mental strain of demands.

clue.text: Arse raving about head of state – Trump's main state

indicators.note: raving is wild and incoherent, so the letters are thrown into disorder
the head of a word is its top, its first letter
the main part leads, so only the opening letter is taken
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A ranting idiot raves about a head of state, apparently Trump's chief concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' appears twice: the first is mined for a letter, the last is the verb being defined. Arse is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert something is to declare it firmly, which is what stating a claim means.

clue.text: Lug married Pole?

blocks.note: to lug something is to tote it
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: Has a big lout wed a Polish woman?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' is capitalised to suggest a Polish person; it is a carved post. A lug is a clumsy oaf in the surface but a verb meaning carry here.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem pole is a carved wooden post, and totem alone can stand for the whole thing.

clue.text: Males pissed about nothing – they're helpless!

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order
to be about something is to surround it on all sides

blocks.note: taken as written
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: Drunk men making a fuss over nothing are hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang pissed means drunk, not angry, and a duck is a batsman's score of zero in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A lame duck is an idiom for a person or concern unable to cope without help.

clue.text: Unnatural language of peers raving on at "stupid ....!"

indicators.note: raving is frenzied and incoherent, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lords ranting away at somebody, with the swear words politely dotted out.
explanation.walkthrough: Peers are members of the House of Lords; 'raving on at' looks like a phrasal verb but splits into signal and letters. The dotted gap is the unprintable insult, adding nothing to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is a constructed international tongue invented in the 1880s, not one that evolved among speakers.

clue.text: River Republican – prepare to do a hatchet job?

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican

blocks.clueFragment: prepare to do a hatchet job
blocks.note: to hone a hatchet is to sharpen it ready for use

explanation.surface: A Republican on the river is getting ready to savage someone's reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: A hatchet job is a vicious attack in print, but read literally it is chopping, which needs a sharpened blade.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône is a major European waterway flowing from Switzerland through France to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Spare broadcaster going round boozer

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: Sky is a British satellite television company
a boozer is British slang for a pub

explanation.surface: A spare presenter heads round to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare' looks like an adjective meaning extra, but here it means lean. Sky is a British broadcaster, and a boozer is a pub, not a drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare describes a body that is lean and thin, with no excess flesh.

clue.text: Stoned, noticing nothing – not yourself, apparently

indicators.note: someone stoned is high and muddled, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: So high you notice nothing and feel like someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not yourself' suggests being unwell or out of it, but here it means appearing to be someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling under a false identity means you seem to be another person, not who you really are.

clue.text: Well, you shouldn't be on this

definitions.text: Well, you shouldn't be on this

blocks.clueFragment: Well, you shouldn't be on this
blocks.note: surface reading: a mild reproach, 'well' as a filler word before a warning
setter's reading: if you are healthy, you have no business being on the register of absent invalids

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' at the start reads as a throat-clearing interjection, but it is the adjective meaning healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: This roster records staff or crew off duty through illness, so a healthy person should not appear on it.

clue.text: (& 6dn) Liberal Nick (drunken lug) being acquiescent

indicators.note: a liberal reading is loose and free, so the letters are not kept in order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg, Liberal Democrat leader, cast as a drunken oaf for going along with the Conservatives in coalition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal Nick' points at Nick Clegg, but 'Liberal' is the signal and both 'drunken' and 'lug' are letters, not description.
explanation.definitionFit: To knuckle under is an idiom for submitting or yielding to pressure, so doing it means giving in meekly.

clue.text: Legendary Labour survivor

blocks.note: surface reading: a long-serving politician of the British Labour Party who outlasted every purge
setter's reading: the mythical strongman who came through twelve impossible tasks set as penance

explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised 'Labour' suggests the British political party; it is one of the twelve feats imposed on the Greek hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The demigod of myth completed the twelve tasks and lived, making him the original survivor of such ordeals.

clue.text: Thinking man's a tosser to be distressed about Conservative leader

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is taken
something distressed is knocked about, so the letters are disturbed
to be about something is to surround it

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An intellectual is a jerk for getting upset about the Tory leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thinking man's' suggests a phrase like 'the thinking man's crumpet', but the 's is just 'is'. Tosser is British slang for a contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian philosopher is the archetypal thinker of the ancient world.

clue.text: Crazy hours with date, making stiff covering?

indicators.note: crazy means wild and unhinged, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: Long late hours with a partner leave someone in a rigid outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like an adjective, but it is slang for a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A shroud is the cloth wrapped round a dead body for burial, and a stiff is slang for a corpse.

clue.text: Staff, getting half-digested food, come together

blocks.note: cud is food brought back up by cattle to chew again
people or ideas that gel come together

explanation.surface: Employees served barely processed canteen food somehow unite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees but is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A cudgel is a short thick stick used as a weapon, a sense of staff as a wooden rod.

clue.text: (& 22dn.) Peanuts and small measure of drink used to imply a small penis?

definitions.text: used to imply a small penis?

blocks.note: peanuts is slang for a very small amount, little
a finger of whisky is the depth of a finger's width in the glass

explanation.surface: Snacks and a small tot of whisky become a mocking gesture about a man's endowment.
explanation.walkthrough: Waggling the smallest digit is a jeering gesture suggesting a man is poorly endowed. 'Peanuts' looks like bar snacks but means a paltry amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding up or waggling the smallest digit is a familiar mocking sign insinuating inadequate size.

clue.text: see 21dn.
Stiff "tackle"? Primitive instincts

blocks.note: a ship's rig is its tackle of ropes and sails
the id is Freud's term for the primitive instinctual part of the mind

explanation.surface: A crude joke: an aroused man's 'tackle' and his base urges.
explanation.walkthrough: Tackle is British slang for male genitals, which the quotation marks wink at; here it is equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigid and stiff are direct synonyms for something that will not bend.

clue.text: Dumb English studies to take precedence

indicators.note: taking precedence means going first, so that piece is placed in front

blocks.note: a den is a private study
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Thick English students insist on being put first.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue the other way round; the instruction puts the rooms in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Dense and dumb are both informal words for stupid, slow to understand.

clue.text: Which tempts surfers to get on well sexually with Harry?

blocks.note: two people who click hit it off, often romantically
to harry someone is to bait or harass them

explanation.surface: Gossip that lures online readers with hints of Prince Harry's love life.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised 'Harry' suggests Prince Harry, a staple of tabloid gossip, but it is the verb meaning harass. Surfers are web users, not people on boards.
explanation.definitionFit: Clickbait is sensational online content designed to lure web users into following a link.

clue.text: Dismay when one meets Putin's top ally

indicators.note: the top of a word written down is its first letter

blocks.note: A means one, as in 'a dog'
the first letter of the name
a pal is a friend or ally

explanation.surface: Horror when someone is introduced to the Russian president's closest henchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top ally' reads as chief supporter, but 'top' belongs with 'Putin's' and the ally is simply a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal someone is to fill them with horror or consternation, the verb sense of dismay.

clue.text: Standard of UK bonking decline?

blocks.note: bonking is British slang for sex, a physical union
to flag is to tire and decline

explanation.surface: Is Britain's sexual performance flagging?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' looks like a level of performance; it is a banner. Bonking is British slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a banner, and the Union Flag (often called the Union Jack) is Britain's national one.

clue.text: Press cooked up lie about politician

indicators.note: a story cooked up is concocted, so the letters are made into something new
to be about something is to surround it

blocks.note: taken as written
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: The newspapers fabricated a falsehood about a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the newspapers, but it is the verb meaning urge.
explanation.definitionFit: To press someone to act is to urge or drive them forward, which is to impel them.

clue.text: "Clout Labour!" a Theresa-Boris thing?

blocks.note: clout is influence or power
to labour is to struggle

explanation.surface: A rallying cry to beat the opposition, attributed to the Conservative rivals at the top.
explanation.walkthrough: Theresa May and Boris Johnson fought over leadership of the Conservative Party. 'Clout Labour!' reads as an order to hit the opposition party.
explanation.definitionFit: Their rivalry for the premiership was an example of a fight for control, hence the question mark.
